q: A red wine shows barnyard, leather and sticking-plaster aromas that deepen in bottle. Which organism is the likely cause?
opts: Botrytis cinerea
Acetobacter
Brettanomyces
Flor yeast
exp: Brett is a yeast whose compounds read as farmyard, leather or sticking plaster. Opinion divides on trace levels; at higher levels it flattens fruit.

q: What is the primary purpose of sulphur dioxide in winemaking?
opts: To deepen the colour of a red wine in barrel
To act as antioxidant and antimicrobial
To convert malic acid into softer lactic acid
To sweeten the wine just before bottling
exp: Sulphur dioxide guards against oxidation and unwanted microbes. Managing it well is much of what keeps a wine stable from cellar to glass.

opts: Fining agents settle particles; filtration strains them
Filtration always takes place before fermentation
They are the same process under two different names
Fining is used only on red wine, filtration only on white
exp: Fining agents attract suspended matter into larger particles that fall out. Filtration passes wine through a physical medium. Many wines see one, both or neither.

q: Two bottles carry the identical protected regional name, one thrilling and one thoroughly dull, and neither producer has broken any rule. What does that name actually guarantee?
opts: That the wine reached a minimum standard of flavour, a score having been awarded to it before release
That the wine will reward several years of cellaring
That the producer owns vineyards rather than buying fruit in from other growers
That the fruit grew inside the named boundary and the rules were followed
exp: A protected name is a claim about a place and about compliance, and compliance is auditable in a way deliciousness is not. Within those limits the range from grower to grower stays enormous, which is why a buyer who knows only the appellation still knows very little.

q: Early wine laws did nothing but draw a boundary on a map, and thin, poorly made wine went on carrying celebrated names quite lawfully. What did the next generation of laws add?
opts: Rules on how the wine had to be grown and made
A requirement that every bottle state its alcoholic strength
A ban on exporting wine outside the country of origin
A minimum selling price for each named region, fixed annually by the state
exp: A boundary answers where and says nothing about how, so a grower could crop enormously, pick unripe and still use the name. Binding production rules to the map is the single step that turned a delimitation into an appellation, and every modern European system rests on it.

q: Frost cuts a village crop to a third, and the grower blends what survives with fruit from parcels entitled only to the wider regional name. Which way may a wine move between two appellations nested inside one another?
opts: Upward into the tighter name, but never downward
Downward into the broader name, never upward into the tighter one
Neither way, since a parcel is fixed to one name for good
Either way, provided the fruit is genuinely from the region
exp: Declassification is always available because the broader rulebook is the easier one to satisfy, and every hectare inside a village sits inside the region as well. The reverse is impossible by construction, which is the practical test of which of two overlapping names sits above the other.

q: One appellation covers an entire region and a second covers a single village lying inside it. Which of the two rulebooks will be the stricter?
opts: Whichever of the two was written more recently
The regional one, since a rulebook covering many more growers has to be written more strictly
The village one, since the rules tighten as the area narrows
Neither, since both rulebooks are approved by the same authority
exp: Yields fall, minimum ripeness rises and the list of permitted grapes usually shortens with every step inward. That is what makes a narrow name worth having: it costs the grower something to use it, and the cost is the information the buyer is paying for.

q: Before a new wine name may be protected, its supporters have to establish something more than that the wine is well made. What must they show?
opts: That the wine has won awards over three consecutive vintages
That the region already exports a substantial quantity, and has done so for many years
A demonstrable link between the place and the character or reputation of its wine
That every grower in the zone has signed the application
exp: The whole legal theory of a geographical indication is that the ground, the climate and the local way of working leave a mark on the character and the reputation of the wine that a buyer can rely on. No link means no case, however good the wine, which is why applications rest on soil surveys, climate records and documented history rather than on tasting notes.

q: A grower crops at half the permitted maximum, picks far riper than the minimum and holds the wine twice as long as required. How does the law treat that?
opts: It is permitted, since the rules fix outer limits
It requires prior written permission from the appellation body
It is permitted only for producers above a certain size
It voids the appellation, because the wine no longer matches the rulebook
exp: A rulebook fixes the widest yield and the lowest ripeness a name will tolerate, so a producer may be as strict with himself as he likes. A few rulebooks do cap alcohol or fix a window for bottling, but the general asymmetry is why the best estates in a region are usually far inside the limits and why the limits themselves tell you about the floor far more often than the ceiling.

q: Brands are bought, sold, licensed and carried across borders every day, and a protected wine name can do none of those things. Which difference accounts for that?
opts: A trademark belongs to one owner and a protected name to no one at all
A trademark lasts ten years and a protected name lasts fifty
A trademark is registered nationally and a protected name internationally
A trademark protects a logo and a protected name protects a word
exp: Nobody owns an appellation, so it cannot be assigned, and it cannot travel because its entire content is where the fruit grew. Any grower inside the boundary who meets the rules may use it, and no grower outside may, however much they pay.

q: A sparkling wine made in England is labelled with a protected French wine name followed by the words style, produced in Sussex, so no buyer could be deceived about where it came from. Why is that still unlawful in the European Union?
opts: It would be lawful if the French name were printed smaller than the English one
Protection extends to evocation, so disclosing the true origin is no defence
It is unlawful only for sparkling wine and permitted for still wine
It becomes lawful as soon as the wine is exported outside the Union
exp: The regulation closes off translation, transliteration and the words style, type, method and imitation alongside outright misuse. The test is whether the protected name is being called to mind at all, not whether any particular buyer was actually deceived, so an honest statement of the true origin makes no difference to the outcome.

q: Wine names won formal recognition as a species of intellectual property, sitting alongside patents and trademarks, in a world trade agreement concluded in 1994. Which agreement?
opts: The Madrid Protocol, which handles trademark registrations
The Bretton Woods agreement
The TRIPS agreement of the World Trade Organization
The Treaty of Rome, which founded the European Economic Community in 1957
exp: Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights, administered by the World Trade Organization, obliges member states to give geographical indications legal means of protection, and it singles out wine and spirits for a stricter standard than other goods. It is the reason a producer in a country with no appellation tradition of its own can still be stopped from using a European wine name.

q: Somebody applies to register the name of a famous wine village as a trademark for wine made a thousand miles from it. What is the usual outcome?
opts: Refusal, but only if a producer from that village formally objects
Refusal, because a mark that misleads the public about geographical origin cannot be registered
Registration, provided the applicant adds a disclaimer to the label
Registration, since trademark law and origin law are separate systems that take no account of one another
exp: Deceptiveness as to origin is a standing ground of refusal in most trademark systems, quite apart from any protected indication. Where a mark was registered long before the indication existed, the two are usually allowed to coexist, which is how a handful of odd historical pairings survive.

q: One kind of protection lapses if its holder stops using it and neglects to renew, while the other runs on for as long as the place and its rules exist. Which is the one that lapses?
opts: The trademark
Neither ever lapses
The geographical indication
Both lapse together
exp: A registered mark has to be renewed periodically and can be revoked for non-use, because it is private property that its owner is expected to work. A registered indication has no expiry date and no owner to abandon it, so it survives changes of hand and generations of growers, though the Union may still cancel a name whose specification stops being met or under which nothing at all has been sold for seven consecutive years.

q: Until the reform that took effect in 2009, European labels divided into quality wine produced in a specified region and table wine. What replaced that split?
opts: A framework of protected designations of origin and geographical indications
A points system in which official panels scored every wine before release
Purely national classifications, with the European layer abolished
A four-tier system written specifically for wine and used nowhere else
exp: Wine was given the same pair of categories the food scheme already used for Parmigiano Reggiano and Prosciutto di Parma, and the two strands have since been drawn into one European register and, since 2024, one regulation. Nothing on the ground moved when it happened: the zones and rulebooks already in force were carried straight across into the new categories, so the reform was a change of framework rather than of boundary.

q: A protected designation of origin requires its grapes to come from inside the named zone. What proportion?
opts: Every one of them
At least half
At least seventy-five percent
At least eighty-five percent
exp: Origin is absolute at this level, and it is the sharpest line between the two protected categories: the broader indication tolerates a fifteen percent margin from outside its boundary while the designation tolerates none. The rules on production and processing tighten in step.
